# Psalm 79: research notes, verse by verse

**Gaps:** I didn't find anything from wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed, LCMS/1517, Pentecostal sites (apart from Enduring Word), netbible, bibleodyssey, Orthodox sites, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this psalm. So those views are missing below. The real disagreements I found are about dating, the curses in vv. 6, 10 and 12, and what "former iniquities" means in v. 8. They are between individual teachers, not clearly between denominations. Spurgeon's Treasury of David page came back empty when I opened it, so his material below comes only from search snippets.

## Introduction: date and author (a real disagreement)
- **Guzik (Enduring Word, which you list under Pentecostal):** clearly written after the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonian armies, so this is likely a later Asaph. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-79/
- **Clarke (Methodist):** the title must mean a later Asaph, his family, or a choir named after him. David could not be its author. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/psalms/79.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** some date it to Shishak's invasion and some to the Maccabees. But Jerusalem was not destroyed in the Maccabean period, so the general voice of commentators favours the Babylonian date. One Pulpit writer, S. Conway, says we need not be at pains to fix the date. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-79.html
- **Matthew Henry (Presbyterian):** reports two views. Some think it was penned long before by the spirit of prophecy; others think it was written at the time by a prophet named Asaph. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_079.cfm
- **Augustine (Catholic):** reads it as a prophecy sung in David's time, before the temple was even built. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801079.htm

## v. 1
- Ellicott: "inheritance" probably intended to embrace both land and people. Benson finds three calamities in the verse: the land taken from God, the sanctuary profaned, the beloved city laid waste. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/79-1.htm
- Pulpit: the Babylonians defiled the temple by breaking in, seizing its treasures and burning it, as the prophets had foretold. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-79.html
- Calvin (Reformed), quoted by Hengstenberg: "the order of nature is, as it were, inverted; the heathen have come into the inheritance of God." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/heg/psalms-79.html
- Matthew Henry: God's own people had defiled it by their sins, and therefore God suffered their enemies to defile it by their insolence. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_079.cfm
- Gill (Baptist) applies it more widely: to Antiochus, the Romans, and the Papists as later invaders of God's heritage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/79-1.htm
- Spurgeon (Baptist) applies it to the church: It is an awful thing when wicked men are found in the church and numbered with her ministry. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-79.html

## vv. 2–3
- Spurgeon: the plea rests on God owning what was harmed. Note "thine inheritance," "thy temple, thy servants," and "thy saints." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/79.htm
- Guzik, citing VanGemeren: the people deserved judgment, yet they are still called God's servants and saints. Citing Kidner: lying unburied was the final humiliation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-79/
- Pulpit: the long siege left many dead around the city. Most people were taken captive, so the few left could not bury the bodies (compare Jer. 14:16). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-79.html
- Augustine (Catholic): "like water" means abundantly. Read of the heavenly Jerusalem, "round about" stretches across the whole earth. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801079.htm

## v. 4
- An older writer quoted by Spurgeon: Of all outward judgments this is the sorest, to have strangers rule over us. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-79.html
- Guzik: the fall made Israel a disgrace among the nations around it. He quotes Spurgeon that delighting in others' misery is worthy only of the devil. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-79/

## v. 5
- Guzik: "How long" asks *when* the suffering will end, not *why* it came. This is a sign of faith, not atheism, because he still addresses God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-79/
- Pulpit: God's jealousy was aimed especially at Israel's worship of other gods, which the exile punished. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-79.html

## vv. 6–7 (curses: disagreement below)
- Pulpit: these are nations that heard of God but refused to "know" him. Quoting Hengstenberg: judgment begins at God's house and then moves on to the nations God used to punish it. vv. 6–7 match Jeremiah 10:25 almost word for word, and it is hard to tell who quoted whom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-79.html
- Guzik: God answered when the Medes and Persians conquered Babylon. Babylon devoured Jacob and was in turn devoured. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-79/
- Spurgeon: in effect the prayer says, if God must pour out wrath, begin with those who have no measure of regard for thee and spare his people. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps079.cfm
- Augustine: Jacob's "place" is probably the city where the temple stood. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801079.htm

## v. 8 ("past sins": real disagreement)
- **Calvin (Reformed):** not just the fathers' sins, nor just youthful sins. It is an acknowledgement that they had for a long time been involved, along with their fathers, in manifold and old transgressions. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/79-8.html
- **Barnes (Presbyterian):** mainly the iniquity of the nation as committed in former times. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/79-8.htm
- **Gill (Baptist):** gives several readings. It could be Adam's sin and original sin, sins of youth, or the ancestors' sins (one Jewish saying links it to the golden calf). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/79-8.htm
- **Another commentary on the same page:** the poet does not mean a guiltless generation is paying for its fathers. He prays as one who has turned away from their sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/79-8.htm
- **Pulpit and Hengstenberg:** they read the Hebrew as "iniquities of our forefathers," on the basis of Leviticus 26:45. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-79.html
- Barnes: "prevent" (KJV) means "go before," that is, come in before ruin becomes certain. Clarke: "brought very low" is literally "greatly thinned." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/79-8.htm

## v. 9
- Spurgeon: This is masterly pleading. No argument has such force as this. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps079.cfm
- Pulpit: the word is literally "make atonement," meaning cancel or forgive the sins. They ask help for God's glory, not because they deserve it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-79.html
- Guzik: the temple and altar were gone, so the psalmist looks for a greater atonement that only God can supply. He links this to Genesis 22. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-79/
- A Pulpit homily calls the gospel the great answer to this prayer: sins forgiven for his Name's sake. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-79.html
- A sermon by R. Tuck: sin must be "covered over" and also "purged away." https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/79-9.htm

## v. 10
- Pulpit: in the ancient world, beating a nation counted as beating its gods. The judgment came only after many years. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-79.html
- Guzik: Asaph asks God to act as the *goel*, the family "avenger of blood." Quoting Horne, this is to vindicate God's character, not to satisfy a vindictive spirit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-79/
- Augustine: the clause is really for the nations' own sake, because those who give up on the true God come to a bad end. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801079.htm

## v. 11
- Guzik, citing VanGemeren: this echoes God hearing Israel's groaning in Egypt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-79/
- Pulpit: "condemned to death" is literally "children of death." It can mean people sentenced to die, or people who will not live long now that they are torn from home. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-79.html
- Benson: "strength" is literally God's "arm." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/79-12.html

## v. 12 (sevenfold payback)
- Benson: "sevenfold" means abundantly, or so that it falls heavily on them. Barnes and Ellicott: the "bosom" is the fold of a robe used as a pocket. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/79-12.html
- Matthew Henry: This prayer is a prophecy, like Enoch's in Jude 15. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/79-11.html
- Augustine: render it "into their bosoms" means rebuke them fully in their secret places. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801079.htm

**The main disagreement over the curses (vv. 6, 10, 12):**
- **S. Conway (Pulpit):** these psalms have ever been a stumbling block to Christian readers. He says they were not wrong for Israel, which had no clear teaching on final judgment, but would be wrong for Christians. Christians should aim such prayers at spiritual enemies instead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-79.html
- **Pulpit (main notes):** these may be official rather than personal feelings, prayers against national enemies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-79.html
- **Guzik and Spurgeon** accept the prayer as concern for God's honour, because the nations mocked God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-79/
- **GotQuestions** lists Psalm 79 among the imprecatory psalms, which are psalms that call down judgment. https://www.gotquestions.org/imprecatory-psalms.html

## v. 13
- Matthew Henry: even brought low, "we are the sheep of thy pasture," not disowned and cast off by thee for all this. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/79-11.html
- Guzik, quoting Boice: this is a faith-filled look ahead to a brighter day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-79/
- Bible Hub study notes link it to Psalm 78:52 and John 10:11. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/psalms/79.htm
- Augustine: "we your people" means all true Christians, so that those who boast may boast in the Lord. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801079.htm
